summary: Adds new cipher suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS) that use the SEED block cipher for bulk encryption. This lets TLS implementations choose SEED as an alternative cipher. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Two computers choose a secret code before whispering. This memo adds one more code, called SEED, to the menu they can choose from.

subtitle: Six new TLS cipher suites that use the SEED block cipher for bulk encryption.

tldr.problem: TLS needed a way to negotiate SEED, a block cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and widely used in South Korea, as the bulk cipher for protecting data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six cipher suites that all use SEED in CBC mode with SHA-1 in an HMAC construction, and differ only in the certificate type and key exchange method.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations can offer SEED as an alternative to other bulk ciphers. The RFC says the new suites are not believed to be less secure than the corresponding older ones. It has since been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015.

today: RFC 4162 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015, so read it together with those documents. The RFC itself describes SEED as widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services.

sections.title: Why Add SEED to TLS
sections.content:
RFC 4162 proposes new cipher suites for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol so that the SEED encryption algorithm can be used as the bulk cipher. The bulk cipher is the part that encrypts the actual application data once the two sides have agreed on keys.

The RFC is short. It does not change the TLS handshake itself. It only defines six new named combinations of algorithms that a client and server can pick from, using the TLS version 1.0 specification in RFC 2246 as its base.
sections.eli5: When two computers talk secretly they pick a lock style from a menu. This memo adds one new lock style, SEED, to that menu.

sections.title: The SEED Cipher
sections.content:
SEED is a symmetric encryption algorithm developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and a group of experts, beginning in 1998. Its input and output block size is 128 bits and its key length is also 128 bits. It has a 16-round Feistel structure: a 128-bit input is split into two 64-bit blocks, and the right 64-bit block goes into a round function together with a 64-bit subkey produced by the key schedule.

The RFC says SEED is easy to implement in software and hardware, and can be used in restricted environments such as mobile devices and smart cards. It describes SEED as a national industrial association standard that is widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services on wired and wireless PKI. The algorithm itself and its object identifiers are described in RFC 4009.
sections.eli5: SEED is a way of scrambling messages in chunks, mixing each chunk over and over in 16 rounds, like shuffling a deck of cards many times.

sections.title: The Six Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Each cipher suite is a two-byte code. RFC 4162 defines six, with values from 0x00, 0x96 through 0x00, 0x9B. Their names follow the TLS pattern of key exchange, then cipher, then hash: for example TLS_RSA_WITH_SEED_CBC_SHA.

All six use the same cipher and hash. They differ only in the kind of certificate and key exchange method, so a server can choose the one that matches the certificates it holds.
sections.eli5: There are six menu items. They all use the same SEED lock, but each one agrees on the secret key in a slightly different way.

sections.title: Cipher, Hash and Key Exchange
sections.content:
The cipher is SEED in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode, a 128-bit block cipher with a 128-bit key. The hash is SHA-1 used in an HMAC construction, as described in section 5 of RFC 2246.

The key exchange algorithms are RSA, DH_DSS, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DHE_RSA and DH_anon. The RFC does not redefine them. It points to sections 7.4.2 and 7.4.3 of the TLS specification for their meaning.
sections.eli5: The lock is SEED, a stamp checks nothing was changed, and the six menu items are six ways of secretly agreeing on the key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it is not believed the new suites are less secure than the corresponding older ones, and that no security problem has been found on SEED. It says SEED is robust against known attacks, including differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis and related key attacks, and that it has been evaluated and considered cryptographically secure by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 and Japan CRYPTREC.

It also notes that SEED had been submitted to other standardization bodies, including ISO (ISO/IEC 18033-3) and the IETF S/MIME work, where it was under consideration. For everything else, the reader is referred to the security considerations of the older TLS and AES cipher suites in RFC 2246 and RFC 3268.
sections.eli5: The authors say experts have tried hard to break SEED and have not managed to. For other worries, you look at how the older locks were checked.
